item.title: Setting up a 44Net Network at Home
item.description:
Goals

This project is part of a larger project related to learning how to integrate the internet with radio. As I learn more and build out the pieces of that project I will try to document them here.

This project has three goals:

  • Learn more about the 44 net
  • Build skills in creating and managing subnets, including firewall management
  • Create a separate network for my AllStarLink, WPSD, and other radio related devices

Prerequisites

  • An Amateur Radio License (you will need to upload an official copy of your license to validate your eligibility to participate in 44net.)
  • Some knowledge/skill in network administration
  • Comfort on the commandline
  • at least two devices that can be used to create this network. I used a Raspberry Pi 3B+ and it worked fine.
    • I installed a basic Debian OS on the device using the Raspberry Pi installer program on my Mac. My ‘second’ device was actually a switch that served four other computers. These were only for testing.
  • Patience

item.title: Recovering From a Failure of my Truenas OS Drive
item.description:
There’s nothing quite like waking up to find that the server that you rely on for most of your services, and on which you store your writing, is not responding and is making that sickening clicky noise that says “dead drive”. Welp, that was my morning.

Now I’ve only been using Truenas about a year so I’m not really familiar with a lot of the nuances of managing these kinds of events. I was very concerned that the process was going to be long, convoluted, and would end up borking my data.

item.title: Ham Radio is Not Dying, It is Evolving
item.description:
Every so often I run across an article or video lamenting the imminent death of Amateur Radio. These folks generally point to how radio has changed over the last few decades as the internet and cellphones have gained prominence in our lives. They argue that the ubiquity of those devices have opened up a world of communication that once was almost solely the domain of radio. Specifically ham radio.

And it’s true: Cellphones and the internet have made communicating with almost anyone, anywhere in the world simple. Moreover, the quality of the connection, the sound quality and so on are excellent and immediate. As an online instructor I had students all over the world. Using the school’s VOIP phone system I could talk with students in Saipan as easily as I could a student down the street. And the quality was excellent with little to no jitter or delay. Truthfully, the same cannot be said for communicating around with world with radio. Atmospheric conditions, sadly, play a large role in the quality of the connection with radio.
